transcript:
Header: 2026-12-14 16:00 PST | Duration: ~46 minutes | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (Kestrel Head of ML Infra), Emma Liu (CTO), Noah Greene (Platform Eng), Ava Torres (Security)

Summary: quick discovery on Dedicated reserved capacity; major themes: isolation/data controls, reserved GPUs + burst strategy, autoscale expectations, latency vs cost, benchmarking and timelines, security/SOC2/KMS.

00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining—I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Daniel, our solutions engineer.
00:06 Raj Patel: Hi all, Raj here. Appreciate you fitting us in, we've been evaluating options for dedicated infra for our LLM features.
00:12 Daniel Ortiz: Great to meet you Raj, Emma, Noah, Ava. Quick agenda, we'll ask about your current stack and workloads, talk about Dedicated (reserved GPUs) and isolation, autoscaling and burst, and then map next steps. Sound good?
00:22 Emma Liu: Sounds good.
00:24 Noah Greene: Yep.
00:30 Raj Patel: Quick context: we're a fintech analytics firm, Kestrel, about 300 engineers. We run a number of LLM-powered features—document summarization, transaction anomaly detection, and chat for support. Currently using hosted endpoints on a mix of managed offerings but we see cost and noisy-neighbor variance. We're exploring reserved capacity to get predictable throughput and isolation for PCI-adjacent workloads.
00:55 Maya Chen: Thanks, that's helpful. Do you have an idea of peak QPS, average seq lengths, and percent of requests that are chat vs embeddings or classification?
01:04 Raj Patel: Peak qps for generation endpoints is about 40 qps right now, average sequence length around 800 tokens for generation, but we have spikes up to 6k tokens for some batch offline workflows. Embeddings qps are smaller but heavy—batched jobs overnight. About 70% of traffic is user-facing chat/generation, 20% embeddings, 10% misc classification.
01:25 Daniel Ortiz: Cool. For Dedicated we generally size based on sustained qps and token throughput. For 40 peak qps at ~800 tokens, that maps to roughly N GPU units depending on model. Do you have a preferred model family or are you exploring open models?
01:40 Raj Patel: We prefer open models for cost and auditability—we're testing Llama-3 family variants and Mistral. Latency SLO is 300-400 ms p50 for shorter queries, but we can accept higher p95 for long sequences. Cost per token is a concern.
01:55 Maya Chen: Understood. A couple things to note: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools with isolation and predictable throughput. We support burst capacity and autoscaling policies—customers can configure a base reserved pool plus a burst pool that can draw from shared spare capacity or cloud instances for short spikes. Burst is priced differently and has limits to avoid noisy neighbor issues.
02:15 Ava Torres: On security—any dedicated option supports VPC-only control plane and customer-managed KMS? We can't have unencrypted key material in vendor KMS.
02:23 Maya Chen: Yes, Private has customer-controlled control plane, but for Dedicated we support bring-your-own-KMS integrations including customer-managed keys via AWS KMS and HSM connectors. We also emit audit logs and per-token tracing for compliance; SOC2 type II docs available.
02:36 Ava Torres: Good, we'll need SOC2 evidence and details on key rotation and audit log retention.
02:40 Maya Chen: We'll share the SOC2 and KMS integration docs after the call.
02:44 Noah Greene: On bursting—what's the typical cold start when you scale up GPUs or spin up burst nodes? We care about tail latency during scale events.
02:53 Daniel Ortiz: For our Dedicated autoscaling, we use pre-warmed images and cached model artifacts. Cold-start to accept traffic is usually in the 30–90s range depending on model size and quantization. For production-critical low-latency paths we recommend a small buffer of reserved capacity to handle the usual spikes. The burst pool is intended for brief surges not sustained throughput.
03:12 Raj Patel: So if we have a sudden 3x spike to 120 qps for a few minutes, how would Redwood behave?
03:18 Daniel Ortiz: Typical setup: base reserved GPUs sized for your 95th percentile steady-state. Then set burst policy to allow up to X additional GPUs for Y minutes. If the burst pool is exhausted we can route to a slightly cheaper compatible model (quantized) as an automatic fallback. Also you can set a queueing policy with SLA thresholds so tail latencies don't blow up.
03:36 Emma Liu: Are those model fallbacks automatic? We need predictable quality—we can't degrade responses unpredictably for user-facing support.
03:45 Maya Chen: Fallbacks are policy-driven. You can opt-in to automatic fallback to a pinned quantized variant for best-effort continuity, or disable automatic fallback and have requests fail fast. We recommend canarying fallback flows during off-peak first.
03:58 Raj Patel: On isolation—do dedicated pools provide single-tenant GPU assignment or is there shared tenancy at the VM level?
04:05 Daniel Ortiz: Dedicated capacity gives single-tenant GPU pools at the shard level—you're not co-located with other customers' models on the same GPU. There may be shared control-plane components, but data plane and model inference run on isolated GPUs.
04:18 Ava Torres: What about network egress and VPC peering? We need strict egress filtering and private subnets only.
04:25 Maya Chen: We support VPC peering and private connectivity. For Dedicated we can ensure nodes live in customer subnets or in a provider VPC with strict peering and firewall rules. We'll capture your network requirements in the follow-up.
04:36 Raj Patel: Also curious about observability—token-level cost, per-route dashboards, tracing hooks?
04:42 Daniel Ortiz: We surface token-level cost, latency heatmaps per model and route, and you can stream traces to your tracing backend. We also have builtin rollback and rollout controls for model versions.
04:50 Raj Patel: Nice. About pricing—how is reserved billing structured vs burst? Monthly commit + overage?
04:56 Maya Chen: Reserved capacity is monthly committed pricing for the GPUs plus a platform fee. Burst is metered separately at a higher rate; there are also commit tiers with discounts. We'll send a SKU/pricing sheet.
05:06 Emma Liu: For benchmarking, we want to run our worst-case flows: long sequence workflows and high concurrency. Can Redwood help with a quick benchmark run?
05:13 Daniel Ortiz: Absolutely. We can run a benchmark on a dedicated test pool or provide a runnable harness you can run in your environment. We'll need your traces and a small dataset.
05:21 Raj Patel: Timeline wise: aim to POC in January, pilot in February, and decision in March. Security signoff is the gating item.
05:28 Maya Chen: That timeline sounds doable—POC using a small dedicated pool and bench runs. We'll include SOC2 and KMS docs and set up the technical deep dive next week.
05:36 Noah Greene: A couple technical clarifications: how do you handle KV cache for long-context models? If we do long sequences up to 6k tokens, we don't want full recompute every request.
05:46 Daniel Ortiz: We support KV cache management; the runtime can preserve per-session KV caches for chat sessions. For Dedicated we persist caches in local GPU memory and can spill to local SSD if needed. Long context is heavier on memory—we'll pick appropriate model/quantization to fit.
05:58 Raj Patel: Any enforced limits on model weights or custom models? We want to run internally-tuned Llama variants.
06:03 Maya Chen: You can bring your own models—customers can upload approved models for Dedicated. We'll validate compatibility and advise on quantization profiles. For private deployments (if you later move to Private) we have a separate package.
06:13 Ava Torres: For compliance, we need log retention to be configurable; cannot retain PII longer than 90 days and must have the ability to redact.
06:22 Maya Chen: We have configurable retention and redaction controls in the console. We'll share the docs.
06:27 Raj Patel: Great. On performance tuning—what knobs do we get? batching, micro-batching, compilation kernels?
06:33 Daniel Ortiz: You get batching configuration, continuous batching, kernel selection heuristics, and quantization recommendations from our Optimize tool. We usually start with conservative batch sizes for latency-sensitive routes and larger batch sizes for background embeddings.
06:46 Emma Liu: Are there SLA commitments for Dedicated? We need uptime and latency SLAs for paid Dedicated tiers.
06:52 Maya Chen: Yes, Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and a latency target window for committed tiers. We'll scope the exact numbers in the proposal based on sizing.
06:59 Raj Patel: Any gotchas we should watch for during POC?
07:01 Daniel Ortiz: Bring realistic traffic traces, include worst-case long sequences, and define your acceptance criteria: p50/p95 latency, throughput, and costs. We'll instrument the run so you can compare to hosted options.
07:13 Maya Chen: Ok to recap next steps?
07:16 Raj Patel: Sure.
07:17 Maya Chen: We'll send: 1) Dedicated pricing + SKU sheet, 2) SOC2 and KMS/HSM integration docs, 3) sample benchmark harness and checklist. Daniel will schedule the technical deep dive to demo autoscaling and burst policies. Kestrel will send traffic traces and SLO targets.
07:35 Emma Liu: Thanks, that works.
07:37 Noah Greene: Thanks everyone.
07:38 Maya Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up on the action items and get the deep dive on the calendar.

End of call.

Notes on transcript quality: medium — auto-transcription had a few swapped product names (e.g., "KV cache" sometimes transcribed as "K-V cash") and punctuation issues.
